To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
social work practice in relation to the detection and management of elder abuse is problematic.
social workers in one area of UK were faced with dilemmas that they were unable to resolve in a way that was ethical or emancipatory.

the social workers interviewed had to work in an environment where they had to deal with complex ethical issues relating to elder abuse in an environment where resources were limited, where the management culture was one that did not encourage the development of emancipatory social work practice and where the social workers themselves did not feel able to challenge the dominant management discourse.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the way in which the social workers' dominant discourse, organisational climate and management priorities interacted with their dilemmas to produce a form of practice that was neither emancipatory nor ethical.
how the dominant discourse and organisational climate of social work agencies can lead to a failure to deal with the abuse of older men and women.

the way in which social workers in the field are constrained in their ability to practice in an emancipatory way by a range of factors, including organisational culture, performance indicators, and lack of resources.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the social work response to elder abuse was inadequate.
elder abuse was an under resourced and poorly understood area of practice, where social workers were faced with dilemmas and were unable to resolve them in the interests of older women and/or men.
social workers in the study area were faced with an impossible task, and that their work was not ethical.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
social workers in the UK are working within a system which has not yet developed an appropriate response to the abuse of older men and women.

the social workers in our study had a strong commitment to ethical practice and to social work values, but that their commitment to ethical practice was undermined by the organisational context in which they worked.

social workers were unable to provide an effective service to older service users because they lacked the resources to do so, and that the organisation in which they worked did little to support or encourage them to do so.
The main takeaway from our work is that

social workers in this area are not being supported to practice ethically in the context of the abuse of elderly women and men, and that the dominant discourse is one of avoidance of ethical dilemmas and of a lack of commitment to emancipatory practice.

the current social policy and organisational climate in which social workers operate is not conducive to ethical practice in elder abuse cases, and this needs to be addressed if the abuse of older people in the community is to be effectively tackled.
social workers are not equipped to work in a climate that is hostile to ethical practice.
